ss03.description: x-height exiters reach ·Tea (full-size bar when a baseline-join follows, else the half stub)

ss04.description: ·It joins at the baseline on both sides at once, any neighbor

ductus.hapax: Begun at the left along the baseline, the stroke runs briefly rightward, then climbs up and to the right in a sigmoid curve and finishes rightward at the x-height.

ductus.full: A single stroke straight down the left from the x-height through the baseline, then a hook out of the foot kicking up and to the right toward the baseline, where it may connect to the next letter.
ductus.half: As the full motion, but only the foot hook is drawn: begun at the baseline on the left, dropping into the descender and kicking back up to the right.

prefer.why: `·Day ~b~ ·Tea` is less pleasant to write than `·Tea ~b~ ·No.alt`
`·Day ~b~ ·Tea` is less pleasant to write than `·Tea ~b~ ·Utter`

ductus.full: The ·Day downstroke and the ·Utter stroke drawn as one motion: straight down the left, hooking out of the descender foot and rising across to exit at the x-height on the right, where it may connect to the next letter.
ductus.half: As the full ligature, but begun from the ·Day foot hook at the baseline, then rising across to the x-height exit on the right.

ductus.hapax: Begun at the left at the x-height, the stroke runs down in a counterclockwise arc and exits at the baseline.

ductus.loop: Written clockwise from the top. Potentially exits at the x-height. Potentially gets joined to at the top height.
ductus.reversed-loop: Joined to at the x-height. Then loops around the bottom and exits at the top, going counter-clockwise.

qsFee.name: qsFee
qsFee.notes: No matter what, ·Fee cannot join both to and from at the x-height on the same letter.

prefer.why: Generally connecting to the next letter is easier to do than to bend ·Fee backwards

ductus.hapax: Begun at the baseline on the left, the stroke climbs up and to the right, almost to the x-height. There, it turns back on itself and draws a small loop clockwise — leftward along the top, down the left side, rightwards at the bottom, and then back to diagonally upwards and to the right — crossing the diagonal it arrived on. It leaves the loop at the upper right and finishes rightward at the x-height.

prefer.why: The `smaller-loop` bitmap doesn’t rub against these letters like the normal one does.

ductus.hapax: - Either written from top to bottom or bottom to top.

refuse.why: ·It never joins to itself. Retires the round-1 entered-it-baseline-join-gain approvals and deliberately forgoes the old font's lone real ·It·It chain (ss04, before ·Utter).
·It·Et looks weird when joined in this font.
Two adjacent verticals joined at the baseline render as one extra-thick stroke.

ductus.hapax: Begun at the left along the baseline, the stroke runs rightward and rises, curls back up and to the left, then doubles back to climb up and to the right, finishing with a short vertical rise that stops at the x-height.

ductus.grounded-loop: Written counter-clockwise, from the rightmost pixel at the x-height. Goes down past the baseline, then loops back a teeny bit at the baseline and then doubles back over itself and exits on the right at the baseline.
ductus.loop: Written clockwise, starting from the leftmost pixel at the baseline, then it continues right, loops around underneath the baseline, and then exits at the x-height on the right.

refuse.why: the old way has ·May make both permissible joins
·Thaw and ·Ye additionally reject the grounded exit when ·May is entered at the x-height.

ductus.flipped: As the loop, but drawn upside down: begun from the lower left, looping over the top, and exiting at the baseline on the right.
ductus.loop: Drawn clockwise from the top left, looping at the bottom, and then exiting on the top right.

prefer.why: I want a word-final ·Tea·Day pair to bind more tightly than the average. This stops `·No.alt ~b~ ·Tea`.

ductus.hapax: A small loop sitting at the x-height, written clockwise from its top, closing on itself; the stroke then runs out diagonally down to the right, ending at the baseline, where it may connect to the next letter. When a previous letter joins at the x-height, the loop opens on the left to receive the join.

ductus.full: Begin at the left, slightly above the x-height; occasionally, another letter will join at the entry, and when the previous letter exits at the x-height, the left upward stroke begins at the x-height instead, dipping down to receive the join. Rise to the top and rightwards in a clockwise curve. Then pull straight down on the right toward the baseline. It may connect to the next letter at the baseline.
ductus.half: As in the full motion, but the downstroke stops at the x-height, or just above it, where it connects to the next letter. When the next letter joins at the x-height, the right downstroke dips down to the x-height to meet it; when letters join at the x-height on both sides, both ends of the stroke dip down to the x-height.

refuse.why: These join ·Pea through the half motion's x-height dip instead; without this refusal the structural floor would pick the lower baseline seam over the half chain.

ductus.hapax:
- Begun at the left at the x-height, the stroke runs rightward, bends down around a shallow bowl on the right, and comes back leftward along the baseline.
- Or the same letter drawn the other way round: begun at the left at the baseline, bending up around the bowl, and finishing leftward along the x-height.
- Either way, when the next letter is to be joined the closing arm turns back out to the right instead of stopping short — running under the bowl when the stroke ends at the baseline, and over it when the stroke ends at the x-height.

qsRoe.name: qsRoe
qsRoe.notes: ·Roe is one stroke between two tips on the left, so whichever tip receives the join, the other is the one that carries on: entering and leaving at the same height is not a shape ·Roe has.

ductus.curled-over: As the normal form, but the crest hooks over and down on the right, exiting rightward to connect slightly above the x-height.
ductus.normal: Begun at the left end of the baseline foot, the stroke runs right along the baseline, rises to the right, snakes back leftward through the waist, and climbs right again into the crest, exiting rightward at the top, where it may connect to the next letter.
ductus.straighter: Begun at the top, the stroke snakes down the spine — leftward through the waist, back out to the right — and then back again to the left a teeny bit by the time it hits the baseline. It may connect to the next letter there.
ductus.straightest: As the straighter form, but the tail finishes straight down onto the baseline.

ductus.hapax: The ·See stroke and the ·Utter stroke drawn as one motion: begun at the crest, the stroke descends leftward down the ·See spine to the x-height, then curves leftward to the baseline. Then the ·Utter part of the stroke retraces part of the ·See part on the way back up and to the right, and eventually breaks out on its own and ends at the x-height, where it may connect to the next letter.

ductus.full:
- Written as a single vertical stroke from the top line straight down to the baseline.
- Or the same stroke, written from the baseline straight up to the top line.
- Under ss03, when the previous letter's stroke arrives at the x-height and the next letter joins at the baseline, the bar is still drawn full-height: the incoming stroke goes up to the top, then doubles back down to the baseline to serve the next letter's join.
ductus.half: As the full motion, but the stroke covers only the span from the top line down to the x-height.

refuse.why: ·Tea and ·It are both vertical, and two adjacent verticals joined at the baseline render as one extra-thick stroke.

unlocks.why: When ss03 is on, I’d rather have `·Ah ~x~ ·Tea.!half` than `·Ah | ·Tea` or `·Ah ~x~ ·Tea.half` — and same thing for other letters (not just ·Ah) that stick out with a flat rightward stroke

ductus.hapax: Written as ·Tea flowing into ·Oy: the vertical bar first, from the top down through the x-height. Without lifting the pen, the small ·Oy loop is drawn clockwise around the foot of the bar, closing on it, and the stroke runs out diagonally down to the right, ending at the baseline, where it may connect to the next letter.

qsTea_qsOy.name: qsTea_qsOy
qsTea_qsOy.notes: Entryless by declaration: the empty entries map is explicit so the obligation is visible (entry inheritance from the lead ·Tea cannot apply — the ligature's leftmost ink at the lead's entry heights does not match the lead's anchors). Predecessors withdraw their exits before this ligature; that is cell semantics on their side, never policy here.

prefer.why: Ligature twin of qsOy.policy.prefer[0] — ligatures do not inherit component policy (proven by u-0283/u-0284/u-0285), and forming ·Tea·Oy must not change the grouping: when the groupings tie, the ligature leaves its baseline exit unrealized so the follower pair joins — "The old way seems nicer to write out by hand".

resolve.why:
Consider ·Tea·Oy·It·No·Ah.

This is the `oy-it-baseline` grouping, but for ·Tea+Oy.

ductus.alternate: Begun at the top, curving leftward and downward, eventually looping around to the bottom right at the baseline. When a previous letter joins at the x-height, the pen will double back over the connecting stroke a bit.
ductus.mono: A short stroke begun at the bottom left, curving upwards and rightwards, to the x-height.

prefer.why: A bare ·Utter before ·May keeps the alternate baseline join; the mono x-height reach into a pulled-back ·May wins only when it buys a better join, as before ·May·May where the grounded ·May carries the chain on at the baseline.
Claude figured that this would be the best (least disruptive) way to have `·Day | ·Utter.alt ~b~ ·Low` happen; The Manual requires this

I want a word-final ·Tea·Day pair to bind more tightly than the average. ·Utter is mentioned here because ·Utter.alt has a mandatory exit, so it can’t help consuming ·Tea’s baseline slot. Only the letter before ·Utter can prevent this.

I want a word-final ·Tea·Day pair to bind more tightly than the average. ·Utter is mentioned here because ·Utter.alt has a mandatory exit, so it can’t help consuming ·Tea’s baseline slot. Only the letter before ·Utter can prevent this.
if `·Utter.alt ~b~ ·May` works, then `·No ~x~ ·Utter.alt ~b~ ·May` should work too; we should have an ·Utter.alt that can connect to the previous letter at the x-height
I would rather have ·Utter.!alt here when the letters around it can connect at either the baseline or x-height and don’t look better or worse one way or the other

refuse.why: “un-”, as a prefix, should not use the alternate ·Utter. It says so in The Manual, on page 21.
